title: Digging into the History of Routes in This Area
text:
Anyone visiting Morton Lochs Nature Reserve can’t help but notice the impressive arched bridge at the edge of the carpark. This puzzling bridge now spans a footpath to one of the bird hides, but 80 years ago, this was the road bridge across the railway line between Leuchars and Tayport. What was the railway line is now one of the main paths through Morton Lochs Nature Reserve.
Curious about the closure of this train line, I asked a local archivist about it, and he pointed me to two fantastic resources.

title: Digging into the History of Routes in This Area
section: The National Library of Scotland Map Viewer
text:
The National Library of Scotland Map Viewer
The first is the National Library of Scotland website, which allows you to compare historic and modern maps. Using the slider bar (at bottom left), you can slide between, for example, the 1888 Ordnance Survey (OS) map (at 100% transparency) and today’s OS map (at 0% transparency), seeing how map features have shifted over the past century. You can zoom in and out and select other historic map overlays as options too!






Figure 2: Image of the NLS site



Click here to access the NLS site yourself.

title: Digging into the History of Routes in This Area
section: The National Records of Scotland Archive
text:
The National Records of Scotland Archive
The second was the National Records of Scotland archive. This amazing dataset showed that the Records of Tayport Burgh, including all the council minutes, were held in the University of St Andrews. So I booked a session in the Napier Reading Room at the Martyrs Kirk Library to go and have a look at these. This beautiful old library on North Street and these old minutes transport you back in time! You can easily lose hours digging through these (chuckling at complaints about unattended dogs).
However, these also showed an investigation into rights of way around the Burgh and a report published by their Sub-Committee on Rights-of-Way. Discussed in the April 1967 minutes, this stated that one of the rights of way beyond the Tayport Burgh was from “Mill Bridge, Shanwell Road to Garpit and Morton Farm and from there to Rhynd Farm”. Looking at the OS map (1:1m to 1:63K, 1920s-1940s), suggests that this route would have followed the yellow line shown:






Figure 3: The Ordnance Survey map from the 1920s-1940s, with a yellow line showing the route that was listed as a right-of-way.



The OS 1:25,000 (Outline), 1945-1965 map shows the same:









Figure 4: The Ordnance Survey map from 1945-1965, with a yellow line showing the route that was listed as a right-of-way.











Figure 5: The Ordnance Survey map from 1945-1965, with a yellow line showing the route that was listed as a right-of-way (continued).






This path is clear on maps as far back as 1798-1878, and 1885-1900. So it seems that this route following beside the old trainline was in fact a right-of-way extending back for more than a century. The current status quo, with no path south from Tayport to the Rhynd is quite a new development for this piece of land, and a path along the route of the old trainline would make a lot of sense to reinstate this lost right-of-way.

title: How it began
text:
🚴️ Tracing the Route of the Tentsmuir Cycle Link
This project began with a simple (and not new) idea: exploring the potential for a new, dedicated route for active travel in our community, connecting Tayport to Leuchars.
I had been working in Denmark for a few years where cycling infrastructure is second to none and had seen first hand the huge benefits to communities in terms of health, well being, reduced congestion and choice that good segregated cycle paths bring. But, living in Tayport,there was a real lack of options for safe cycling locally towards St Andrews, which is an economic hub in this part of Scotland. The main road between Tayport and Leuchars is narrow, busy and has no cycle lanes - not suitable for families or less confident cyclists. The alternative route via Tentsmuir is lovely, but runs along on gravel tracks unsuitable for road bikes and is a significant detour. It seemed crazy not to have a direct safe option, especially when a good route existed between Dundee and Tayport and St Andrews to Leuchars - if we could get a link between Tayport and Leuchars we could connect all these places with a safe, efficient route for cycling and walking.


🗺️ The First Exploration: South from the Larick
I heard through the Tayport community gardens that Mark was well connected to cycle communities. I approached Mark at a meeting in Larick center, asking if anyone had thought about a potential path along the old railway line from Tayport to Leuchars. Turns out indeed many had but there had never been much progress. So Mark, Jim (who Mark introduced me too) and I decided to go for a cold February walk from the Larick Centre, heading south down the Scott & Fyfe road to see if we could follow the old railway line.
While a significant portion of the route was plain sailing, the initial stages required a bit of inventive navigation! We squeezed under a few barbed wire fences, carefully crossed a short stretch of a planted winter barley field (responsibly of course), jumped one ditch, and diverted around a field boundary. Eventually we made to a section of the railway which is relatively well preserved (Morton Lochs also has a great section that’s currently a path) near the Rhynd cafe and from there it was an easy walk to Leuchars.



Part of the old railway in Morton Lochs




🚧 Alternative Route Challenges
In other walks we also explored some alternative routes but these were not always straightforward. Mark and Jim attempted to map an alternative route from the south, which proved to be a chilly lesson in the lay of the land. They were cut off by a high deer fence and gate near Fetterdale. Jim managed to climb the gate, but Mark found it tricky. After they climbed back over, they had to change tack, returning to the Rhynd area. There, they encountered another obstacle—a lower locked gate—which was climbed to finally gain access to the Tentsmuir forest track and get back up to Fetterdale. Despite the cold, they returned pleased, having learned invaluable lessons about the landscape and potential access points.


🏛️ Laying the Groundwork: Consultation and Research
After exploring the possible options on foot Jim and I got on our laptops and started trying to figure out how to make the cycle path a reality. By happy coincidence, Fife Council had just begun a consultation on the Active Travel Strategy and Action Plan. We attended a consultation meeting in the small meeting room at the Larick Centre, which helped us align our vision with the broader local strategy - we submitted our thoughts as a document to the consultation that a direct link between Leuchars and Tayport would be important and the old railway line was an obvious place to start thinking about where a route might go. We then began detailed research:

Landowner Identification: We researched online to find the landowners involved along the route.
Historical Mapping: We poured over maps of the old railway line to trace the forgotten path, a potential alignment for our route.
Formal Submissions: Our initial research culminated in a succesful submission to Fife Council’s Active Travel Strategy.

We also reached out to Cllr Jonny Tepp, asking if he had any advice. His support in making contacts with council officers and with local organisations has been helpful and appreciated


🤝 Building Relationships: Engaging with the Farming Community
In establishing this route it is important that we engage with landowners. While it’s always going to be tricky trying to approach the idea of a path being built on someone’s land, all the landowners we have approached so far have listened to our thoughts and ideas and we hope this forged an initial relationship for future discussions, despite some landowners having serious reservations. Our aim is to work collaboratively and keep them in the loop at every stage.


🌟 Bigger and Team and moving Forward
Our numbers are growing with new team members and we are now a constituted body within Tayport Community Council that can represent the community in Tayport along with Guardbridge and Leuchars.
Our next stage is…well this blog post the new website and community consultation. Once we show community buy-in, Fife council should release the funding for an initial feasibility study and that will push us closer to safer, more accessible active travel for Tayport, Leuchars and North East Fife.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text: Got questions about the Tentsmuir Cycle Link? We’ve answered the most common ones below. If you’d like to ask something else, feel free to contact us.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
About the Route

What is the Tentsmuir Cycle Link?
The Tentsmuir Cycle Link is a proposed cycle and walking path that would connect Tayport and Leuchars, completing a continuous, direct and safe route for cyclists and pedestrians all the way from Dundee to St Andrews.
Cycle paths already exist between Dundee and Tayport, and between Leuchars and St Andrews. This new link fills the missing middle section,approximately 6.7 - 8.9 km (4.2 - 5.6 miles) — running alongside Tentsmuir Forest.


Why does the path run between Tayport and Leuchars specifically?
This section is the critical missing link in an otherwise continuous route from Dundee to St Andrews, two major economic hubs. Currently there is no safe off-road option for this stretch. Cyclists are forced either onto the A914, which is a busy, fast, and narrow road that many people, particularly families, children, and older adults, find far too dangerous or they have to cycle through gravel paths in Tenstsmuir which are not direct and unsuitable for many types of bike and other forms of active travel.
Completing this connection would unlock the entire Dundee–St Andrews corridor for safe active travel.


How long is the proposed route?
The proposed routes between Tayport and Leuchars are approximately 6.7 - 8.9 km (4.2 - 5.6 miles) long depending on whether the more direct railway route or one that passes along the edge of Tentsmuir forest is built. At a relaxed to moderate cycling pace this takes roughly 20–45 minutes.


Where exactly would the path go?
We have identified three potential routes that would run in or alongside Tentsmuir Forest, a beautiful part of Fife. You can explore the proposed routes in detail on our Map page. Our preferred option is the route along the old railway line but this is subject to a feasibility study and runs through private land.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Why Build It?

Why can’t people just use the existing roads?
The current road options between Tayport and Leuchars are unsuitable for most cyclists:

The A914 is a busy, fast-moving road with no dedicated cycling provision and narrow verges.
Many people, including children, families, and older or less confident cyclists, simply won’t use it.
The road also suffers from potholes and poor sightlines in places.

A safe, dedicated off-road path is needed to make cycling a genuine everyday option for local residents, tourists and commuters.


Haven’t bus services recently been cut in the area - wny not spend the money on reinstating those?
Yes. Recent cuts to bus services in Tayport and Leuchars have left many residents with fewer options for getting around without a car. While the cycle path won’t directly replace bus services, it provides an important and reliable alternative for shorter local journeys, particularly to Leuchars railway station, that people can use regardless of timetables or fares. The money ring fenced for cycling cannot be used for more bus services and, even if it could, a cycle path guarantees an alternative option for travel for decades to come, while extra bus services can be withdrawn at any time.


Why don’t we just fix the potholes on the A914 instead?
While fixing potholes on the A914 would be welcome, it wouldn’t address the fundamental safety issues of that road for cyclists. The A914 is a busy, fast-moving road with no dedicated cycling provision and narrow verges. Even if the surface were improved, many people, particularly children, families, and older or less confident cyclists, would still find it too dangerous to use. A dedicated off-road path is needed to make cycling a genuine everyday option for local residents.


What about the farmers and land owners - won’t this negatively impact them?
We made it a priority to engage with the landowners along the proposed routes. We understand that there would be some disruption during construction and then more people would use the paths than currently, but we are committed to working collaboratively to minimise this and ensure that the path is designed in a way that respects the needs of local farmers and landowners. While we understand that landowners have concerns about the path, we believe many of these can be mitigated and the huge benefits to the community outweigh the temporary inconvenience to land owners.
In the long term, the path could provide benefits such as improved access for farm vehicles and increased foot traffic for local businesses.


How would the path help people get to Leuchars railway station?
Leuchars railway station sits on the main Edinburgh–Dundee–Aberdeen rail line and provides fast connections to Edinburgh and beyond. Currently, accessing the station from Tayport without a car is difficult.
The cycle path would make it straightforward to cycle or walk to the station in 20–45 minutes from Tayport, opening up rail travel for commuters and day-trippers who would otherwise need to drive and park.


Would this benefit people who don’t currently cycle?
Absolutely; and that’s one of the main goals. Research consistently shows that people don’t cycle primarily because roads feel unsafe, not because they lack interest. A safe, off-road path removes the biggest barrier. Many people who wouldn’t dream of cycling on the A914 would be happy to use a well-surfaced, segregated path through Tentsmuir.
The path would also be fully accessible on foot, so it benefits walkers, families with buggies, and people with mobility aids too.


Will it bring more visitors to Tayport?
Yes. The path would make Tayport much more accessible by bike from Leuchars, St Andrews, and Dundee. This increased footfall would benefit local shops, cafes, pubs and businesses, providing a boost to the local economy.
It would also give visitors a new and attractive way to access Tentsmuir Forest and Beach — one of Fife’s most popular natural destinations.


Is the route only useful for leisure cycling?
No, the route is designed for everyday transport as well as leisure. It would be a practical option for:

Commuters cycling to Leuchars station or to workplaces in Leuchars (including RAF Leuchars / MOD Leuchars) as well as cyclists who wished to travel between Dundee, Tayport, Leuchars and St Andrews for work or study.
Students and families travelling between communities
Shoppers and visitors travelling between Dundee, Tayport, Leuchars and St Andrews
Recreational cyclists and walkers exploring Tentsmuir

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Environment & Health

How does the path help reduce CO₂ emissions?
Every car journey replaced by a bike ride reduces carbon emissions. Studies have shown that investment in cycling infrastructure can produce significant and sustained reductions in car use. By making cycling a safe and practical choice for everyday trips, the Tentsmuir Cycle Link would contribute to reducing the area’s carbon footprint and help meet Scotland’s climate targets.


What are the health benefits?
Regular cycling and walking improve both physical and mental health. A safe local cycle path encourages more people, including those who currently do very little exercise, to build active travel into their daily routines. This has knock-on benefits for the NHS and for individuals’ long-term wellbeing.


Will the path be good for wildlife?
Overall, yes, but of course, laying a surface suitable for cycling will have some localised negative environmental impacts. However, especially for Option A along the old railway line, much of the path is mostly track anyway and so laying a surface suitable for cycling would have little effect on wildlife. The current fields where cycle path may be constructed are used for crops and mostly do have not hedgerows and therefore are not particularly biodiverse habitats Alongside the path, we would hope to plant native hedgerows and wildflowers; this will support insects, birds and other wildlife — turning the route into a biodiversity asset as well as a transport one.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
The Project

Who is behind this campaign?
The campaign is run by a group of local residents and cycling enthusiasts who want to see Tayport, Leuchars and the surrounding communities better connected by safe active travel routes. We work under the name Tentsmuir Cycle Link and engage with Fife Council and other stakeholders to push the project forward. The group is affiliated with Tayport Community Trust.


Where has the project got to so far?
There has been encouraging progress behind the scenes, including early engagement with Fife Council and local representatives. You can read more about the story so far on our blog.


How can I help?
The single most impactful thing you can do right now is take our survey. Demonstrating local support with real numbers is vital for making the case to Fife Council that this route should be prioritised.

 Take our Survey! 

You can also spread the word by sharing the website with friends, family and neighbours, especially those who live in Tayport, Leuchars and St Andrews.


Who can I contact if I have more questions?
Feel free to get in touch by email; we’d love to hear from you.

title: Route Map
text:
We are working on several different possible routes. Three of the broad options are detailed in the interactive map below. Our preferred option is to follow the old Tayport branch railway line (dashed blue). Any of the routes are subject to change with feasibility, practicality, cost and land owner consent all factors in what is finally built.
Click on any route to see more details. The dashed lines are possible routes and solid lines are existing cycle paths.

title: Route Map
text:
Route details

Option A – Old Railway Line
Distance: 6.7 km | Status: Preferred route
Option A follows the route of the former Tayport Branch Line, which closed in 1966. The trackbed is largely flat and intact, offering a direct, traffic-free corridor between Tayport and Leuchars. Key advantages include:

Minimal road crossings, improving safety for all users.
Low impact on agricultural land compared to the other options.
Likely the least expensive route to construct due to the existing railway line.

This is our preferred option and the one we are advocating for with Fife Council.
Note that land owners currently oppose large sections of this route as it would require use or acquisition of private land - see here for more info.



Option B – Tentsmuir Forest Route: 8.0 km
Distance: 8.0 km | Status: Alternative under consideration
Option B runs through the interior of Tentsmuir Forest before joining the back road to Leuchars. While it avoids some private land it comes with several challenges:

The back road to Leuchars is narrow and would need to be widened at several points which would require agricultural land.
The route is 1.3 km longer than Option A
Road widening works would possibly be more disruptive and costly than the railway option
Sections through the forest may be affected by forestry operations

This option remains a “Plan B” but is not currently preferred.
Note that land owners currently oppose large sections of this route as it would require use or acquisition of private land - see here for more info.



Option C – Tentsmuir Route: 8.9 km
Distance: 8.9 km | Status: Alternative under consideration
Option C is a longer alternative through Tentsmuir suggested by some stakeholders. It shares many of the same challenges as Option B, and is an additional 2.2 km compared to the preferred railway route. A large portion of this route would follow an existing forestry track, which offers some advantage, but:

The overall length makes it less attractive for everyday cycling trips
The start of the route is prone to flooding, which would likely require major works to construct a raised road, increasing costs.
The route does not pass through Morton Lochs and so provides less connectivity.
It still requires road sections as in Option B that would need improvement

This option is retained for completeness but is not preferred at this stage.
Note that land owners currently oppose large sections of this route as it would require use or acquisition of private land - see here for more info.



Active travel strategy
The Tayport Cycle Link forms part of Fife Council’s broader Active Travel Strategyconnecting Fife’s towns and villages with safe cycle routes. You can find more information about the Active Travel Strategy on the Fife Council website.


Map of Fife Council’s Active Travel Strategy showing proposed cycle routes in North East Fife

title: Benefits
text:
We believe the Tentsmuir Cycle Link is a vital piece of community infrastructure that will bring numerous benefits to North East Fife and beyond.

🌱 Connecting our Communities
The Tentsmuir Cycle Link will mean there is a continuous, safe and efficient cycle path from St Andrews to Dundee and beyond. This link between towns such as Tayport and Leuchars, will allow more access to local services without the need to rely on buses, bring more business to Tayport and Leuchars, make safe cycle commuting possible and generally enhance community connectivity in North East Fife.

Providing our communities with transport options
The Tentsmuir Cycle Link will provide an alternative to car travel for many local journeys. This is especially important given the recent cuts to bus services in Tayport and Leuchars - although it won’t replace these services it will provide options for the local community.


Access to Leuchars Railway Station
It will be a roughly 9km (25 - 45 mins) cycle along the cycle path from Tayport to Leuchars railway station. This will make it easier to commute by train to Edinburgh and beyond without the need for a car.


More footfall in Tayport
The cycle path will bring more people into Tayport, especially from Leuchars and St Andrews. This will result in more business for local shops, cafes and pubs.


Options to access Tentsmuir Forest and Beach
The Tentsmuir Cycle Link will provide a safe and efficient way for people to access Tentsmuir Forest and Beach by bike or on foot from Leuchars, Tayport and St Andrews. This will open up this beautiful area to more people without the need for a car.



🛡️ Safer for Everyone
Lots of people are put off cycling by our pot holed and sometimes dangerous roads. Currently the options to cycle between St Andrews and Dundee via Tayport involves either a very busy and narrow road or taking a long detour into Tentsmuir forest on gravel track unsuitable for road bikes. The Tentsmuir Cycle link will provide a continuous, segregated, efficient link for cyclists avoiding busy roads meaning a safer journey for cyclists and less congestion and frustration for cars.


🏃 Boosts Health and Active Lifestyles
Cycle paths encourage more cycling and active travel boosting health. The Tentsmuir Cycle link will encourage community and open up cycling destinations via bike to far more people. It will be a beautiful route passing through forests and countryside and studies show that even just ten minutes in nature can greatly boost mental health and well being.


🌳 A Biodiversity Corridor
We plan on planting native hedges and wildflowers alongside the path encouraging insects, birds and other wildlife and creating a wildlife corridor between Leuchars and Tayport.


🌱 Cuts CO₂ Emissions
Cycle paths take cars off the road and studies have shown they can significantly reduce carbon emissions helping us reach a less carbon-intensive society.

title: Where we are we September 2026
text: After almost two years of working behind the scenes, the website and consultation are finally open! We are really proud to get here and encourage everyone reading to make sure they take the survey—it makes a massive difference.

title: Where we are we September 2026
text:
Why so long?
But why so long to get to this point? The answer to that is that there’s already been a lot happening behind the scenes; for example, exploring route options, getting our cycle path on the Council’s Active Strategy, contacting stakeholders, and particularly trying to engage landowners. Taking a look at the map of possible routes, Option A is our preferred route, but it passes over land belonging to several landowners. Options B and C pass through more public land initially before hitting the back road to Leuchars—if we wanted to widen the road or add a segregated cycle path, this would require private agricultural land too.



The old railway line is a good canditate for a cycle path - and a lot of it is still core path)

title: Where we are we September 2026
text:
Land ownership issues
So all routes require the acquisition or use of private land, and we wanted to get this right from the start by engaging with landowners, asking them what they thought, what issues there might be, and having a process by which we recommended how we thought a path could be built that suited both the rural and wider community. Unfortunately, after a long series of talks, emails, and letters, and a delayed launch due to objections, we were unable to come to a consensus.
The position of the landowners is that a path, particularly Option A along the old railway line, is incompatible with farming operations. Landowners argue that a path would:

disrupt harvest by having cyclists on the path.
disrupt pheasant shooting and stalking deer.
prevent maintenance of ditches.

We have tried to propose potential solutions; for example, the path could be closed during harvest with diversions along the road or through Tentsmuir, or designing a path that allows for easy maintenance of ditches, but this has not resulted in any progress. A large portion of the old railway actually is already a core path that cyclists have a statutory right to use, and we believe that there is a strong community, economic and environmental case for resurfacing to make it more accessible and allowing the community to use the “non-core” section up to Morton Lochs, especially as this used to be a right of way.

title: Where we are we September 2026
text:
What now
So where do we go from here?
The Council is generally very reluctant to use its statutory powers to acquire land, and in some ways for very good reason—it’s a long, drawn-out process that nobody wants and costs a lot of money. They might as well use those funds to build cycle paths elsewhere. So it’s up to us as a community to make it known that we want this cycle path built. The council has already agreed they will begin formal consultations when community support is demonstrated and will take into account views expressed by all sides. Hopefully, if we can demonstrate enough support, the landowners might think again about their objections to the route.

title: Where we are we September 2026
text:
Take the survey!
So in a nutshell, it’s time to demonstrate that our local communities want this cycle link - connecting Dundee, Taypot, Leuchars, Guardbridge and St Andrews with an accessible, safe route for everyone. If you want this to happen then please take our survey!
